P01.convention: a trailing nonrestrictive modifier ('out of a small harbor...') may be set off by a single comma at sentence end
P01.note: Name directly after 'the institute's ship' with no punctuation; A's lone dash never closes, C makes a fragment. The passage stresses the institute had ONE ship, which argues for a nonrestrictive appositive the options never offer, and D's comma before the trailing locative is legitimate.
P01.not_hard_because: C is an obvious fragment and A's unclosed dash is a known never-right shape, leaving a B/D choice that turns on a comma most students skip by default.

P02.note: Plural 'Floods' (first word of clause) needs a plural verb; present perfect fits the present-tense frame ('requires', 'worry'). 'spillway' is the singular attractor.
P02.not_hard_because: the subject 'Floods' opens the clause and the attractor 'spillway' is a single short prepositional phrase, so number is settled at once; 'were carving' has no past anchor.

P03.note: 'the chief ___ graft' needs a possessive; 'chief' signals a single propagator, so singular possessive. D tempts students who default to plural possessive.
P03.not_hard_because: 'chief' before the blank hands over the singular, and A/C leave 'graft' with no grammatical role; nothing beyond one possessive decision.

P04.note: Plural 'Trainees' plus the delayed '-ing' participle 'handling' after the interrupter requires a be-auxiliary ('are ... handling'); 'do' cannot take the participle. 'master's studio' is the singular attractor.
P04.not_hard_because: plural 'Trainees' is the first word of the sentence, so the two singular options fall at sight; only the be/do choice remains and 'handling' is the only verb form in reach.

P05.note: Plural 'names' with 'since the volume entered...' requires present perfect; 'margin'/'sheet' are singular attractors.
P05.not_hard_because: 'since' hands over the present perfect and 'names' is plainly plural, so the 2x2 grid collapses to one cell; same template as P33 and P39.

P06.note: 'first in X, then Y' is a phrase-level sequence: a comma, not a semicolon (no clause follows) or colon (not an explanation). C's missing comma is the closest rival.
P06.not_hard_because: 'first ... then' is a stock correlative that cues the comma; the semicolon and colon need a following clause that obviously is not there.

P07.note: Heavy object shifted after the adverbial: 'set aside for emergency repairs the surplus that...'. Any mark separates verb from its object. B is attractive because the long object 'feels' like it needs a pause.

P08.note: Plural 'readings' and 'in the decades preceding the port's first float-driven gauge' require simple past plural.
P08.not_hard_because: the time phrase 'in the decades preceding' hands over the past and 'readings' is unmistakably plural; 'pier' is a weak attractor.

P09.note: Elliptical clause echoing 'has dwindled': 'the vacancies ... have [dwindled] too'. Needs a have-auxiliary AND plural number; C copies the singular 'has' from the parallel clause, B/D supply 'be', which has no verb to echo.

P10.note: Singular 'director' (attractor 'admissions') takes 'was'; the object is the single 'family's questionnaire', so 'it'.
P10.not_hard_because: both rules point to the nearest singular nouns ('director', 'questionnaire'); 'admissions' is a weak attractor and 'them' has no plural candidate in the sentence; same 2x2 verb-number x pronoun grid as P13, P27, P35.

P11.note: Cataphoric ellipsis: 'the bath usually is [dependable]', borrowing the predicate of the main clause; 'does' has no verb to stand for. Singular 'bath' against plural attractor 'farms'.

P12.note: Compound subject joined by 'and' takes a plural verb; present tense set by 'as long as a bed is not planted'. 'white mustard' is the singular attractor next to the blank.
P12.not_hard_because: 'and' joining two nouns is a textbook plural signal, and the present-tense 'is not planted' clause hands over the tense.

P13.note: Singular 'canister' takes 'is'; the agent is the drones, so 'them'. 'it' tempts because 'battery'/'crust'/'vent' are singular nearby.
P13.not_hard_because: the only things that can tow are the plural drones, and 'a steel canister' is plainly singular; 2x2 grid shared with P10, P27, P35.

P14.note: 'has always ... subsided': the participle is delayed by 'within an hour of the afternoon melt peak'; 'is subsided' is not idiomatic, and 'level' is singular against plural attractor 'charts'.

P15.note: Cataphoric ellipsis echoing 'loses much of its ability': 'samples rarely do [lose...]'. Present simple and plural; 'have' has no participle to echo.

P16.note: A complete clause ('The interviewers' logs recorded what the refusing households had in common') introduces a list, so a colon.
P16.not_hard_because: 'had in common' announces that a list follows, and the three-item list is visibly coming; same colon-after-complete-clause template as P17.

P17.note: Complete clause ('riders weighed a hidden cost more heavily than the ticket price') followed by the specification of that cost: colon. 'a hidden cost' announces what follows.
P17.not_hard_because: 'a hidden cost' cues an explanation, C is garbled, and the semicolon needs an independent clause that is not there; same template as P16.

P18.note: Plural 'cashiers', and 'during the paper-ticket era that preceded student swipe cards' sets past progressive.
P18.not_hard_because: 'during the paper-ticket era that preceded' hands over the past and 'cashiers' opens the clause plural; the singular options attach to nothing.

P19.note: 'Wafers ... were also ... unfit for sale': the predicate adjective is delayed by 'by the inspectors' revised standards'; 'have unfit' is ungrammatical. Plural subject.
P19.not_hard_because: 'Wafers' is the first word and the noun before the blank ('bays') is also plural, so there is no attractor; the only work is finding 'unfit' past the interrupter.

P20.note: 'catalog' is the main verb: 'the archivists catalog entries...'. Possessive readings (C/D) leave the sentence with no verb; B needs 'catalogs'. The noun/verb ambiguity of 'catalog' makes the possessives attractive.

P21.note: Two independent clauses: the second's subject is 'the remedy that physicians ... praised' with verb 'did little'. B reads as an appositive to 'air' until 'did' turns it into a splice; A's colon does not introduce an explanation of the first clause.

P22.note: Plural 'loans' (attractors 'farmer', 'title') with present tense set by 'serves' and 'borrow'.
P22.not_hard_because: the present-tense 'serves' sits right after the blank and 'loans' is plainly plural, so the 2x2 grid collapses at once.

P23.note: Singular 'reel' with present tense from 'whenever a technician threads'.
P23.not_hard_because: 'threads' (present) and the singular 'the final reel' both sit in plain view; the plural options require reading 'feature' as the subject, which nobody does.

P24.note: 'played' is intransitive here; 'the pipes mounted highest...' is the main-clause subject with verb 'sounded'. C's garden-path reading 'played the pipes' is very attractive until 'often sounded' has no subject.

P25.note: Singular 'Turnout' (attractors 'renters', 'blocks') with 'during the mayoral runoff that autumn' setting simple past.
P25.not_hard_because: 'that autumn' hands over the past and 'Turnout' opens the sentence; the plural options need 'blocks' as subject.

P26.note: Possessive needed before 'tally'; the closing sentence ('The contractors later disagreed') makes the contractors plural, so plural possessive. A is the strongest distractor for students who stop at the sentence.
P26.not_hard_because: the next sentence explicitly names 'The contractors' in the plural, handing over the number; B leaves 'tally ... recorded' garbled.

P27.note: Plural 'veterinarians' takes 'have'; the antibody levels are the chicks'/birds', so 'their'. 'its' tempts via 'grower'/'spray'.
P27.not_hard_because: 'veterinarians' is plainly plural and the only plausible owners of antibody levels are the plural birds; same 2x2 grid as P10, P13, P35.

P28.note: Second independent clause: 'a sheltered block ... flowered eleven days later'. A reads as an appositive to 'orchard' until 'flowered' makes it a splice; a colon does not fit since the clause does not explain the first.

P29.not_hard_because: 'shows' after the blank hands over the present, and 'milk' is a mass noun every student treats as singular; 'cows' is far away.

P30.note: Singular 'apprentice' (attractor 'compositors') with past from 'when a candle tipped over'.
P30.not_hard_because: 'when a candle tipped over' hands over the past progressive and 'the newest apprentice' is plainly singular.

P31.note: 'found' takes a that-less noun clause as object ('found [that] the dispensers ... were used'); no mark between verb and object.
P31.not_hard_because: the verb-plus-object-clause pattern is common; comma/dash/semicolon all visibly cut 'found' from what was found. Same no-punctuation-before-object template as P07.

P32.note: Ellipsis echoing 'recalls ... more accurately': 'a student ... often does'. Singular, present. 'formulas'/'mornings' are plural attractors.
P32.not_hard_because: 'recalls' is the only verb to echo and it is present singular; 'was'/'were' have nothing to stand for. Same elliptical-auxiliary template as P09, P11, P15.

P33.note: Plural 'probes' with 'for nine growing seasons' requiring present perfect progressive; 'estate's' is the singular attractor.
P33.not_hard_because: 'for nine growing seasons' hands over the present perfect; same since/for template as P05, P39.

P34.note: 'copied the exemplar' is the subordinate clause (confirmed by 'that model'); comma before the main-clause subject 'the illuminators'. A breaks the verb from its object; C puts a semicolon after a dependent clause.
P34.not_hard_because: 'that model' later points back to the exemplar, handing over that it is the object of 'copied'; mirror image of P24 (same subordinate-clause/object boundary).

P35.note: Plural 'sketches' takes 'depict'; the thing depicted is the single 'original window', so 'it'.
P35.not_hard_because: both rules resolve to the obvious nouns ('sketches', 'window'); same 2x2 grid as P10, P13, P27.

P36.note: Plural 'tracks', and 'on the night of the club's closing concert' sets simple past; the 'since the album first reached record shops' inside the relative clause tempts D's present perfect.

P37.note: Restrictive participle: the specimens gathered along the margin are contrasted with those from the interior, so no comma. A/C would make the location incidental.
P37.not_hard_because: the next sentence's 'by contrast' explicitly names the other group, handing over the restrictive reading; D is an obvious fragment. Same uniqueness/restrictiveness template as P01, P38.

P38.note: 'the observatory's largest dish' is already unique, so the participial phrase is nonrestrictive and takes a comma. B misreads it as 'the largest of the warped dishes'.
P38.not_hard_because: 'largest' hands over uniqueness, so the comma; B is a fragment and D's colon has no list or explanation. Same restrictiveness template as P01, P37.

P39.convention: American edited English accepts simple past for a completed event with present relevance when no time marker conflicts
P39.note: Singular 'optic' (attractor 'panes'); present perfect fits the present-result frame ('the beam ... is whiter'), but nothing excludes a simple past 'was superseded'.
P39.not_hard_because: the number is settled by 'The rotating optic' opening the clause, and the tense choice does not discriminate because C is also acceptable.

P40.note: Singular 'catalogue' (attractor 'photographs') with 'during the slide-rule era's closing years' setting past.
P40.not_hard_because: 'during the slide-rule era's closing years' hands over the past and 'the catalogue' is singular; same past-time-phrase template as P08, P18, P25, P30.

tells: Subject-verb items (P02,P04,P05,P08,P09,P12,P14,P18,P22,P23,P25,P29,P30,P33,P36,P39,P40) are all 2x2 number-by-tense grids: two independent binary rules, each solvable from one cue, so the key is the one cell surviving both.

In those items the noun immediately before the blank is almost always the WRONG number (P02 spillway, P05 sheet, P08 pier, P09 board, P10 admissions, P12 mustard, P14 borehole, P22 title, P23 feature, P25 blocks, P30 room, P39 panes, P40 photographs); 'skip the nearest noun, take the first noun of the clause' picks number nearly every time. Exceptions: P19, P29, P33.

Tense is always handed over by a time phrase AFTER the blank: past by 'during ...'/'in the decades preceding'/'that autumn'/'when ...' (P08,P18,P25,P30,P40), present perfect by 'since'/'for N seasons' (P05,P33), present by a present verb in a trailing clause (P22,P23,P29). Only P36 plants a decoy 'since'.

Pronoun items (P10,P13,P27,P35) are all 2x2 verb-number x pronoun-number grids; the pronoun's correct referent is always the semantically obvious actor/object and the wrong one is always a nearby noun of the other number.
Boundary items with a clause after the blank (P21,P28) both use 'noun, the/a NP ... verb' where the comma option is an appositive garden path and the key is the full stop/semicolon.
Subordinate-clause object boundary (P24,P34): both hinge on whether the noun after the verb is its object; solving one transfers directly.
Elliptical auxiliary items (P09,P11,P15,P32): key is always the auxiliary that echoes a verb elsewhere in the sentence; options supplying an auxiliary with no echoed verb always lose.
Colon items (P16,P17): a complete clause ending in an announcing noun ('had in common', 'a hidden cost') always takes the colon.
Restrictiveness items (P01,P37,P38): a uniqueness/contrast cue in the passage ('the same ship', 'largest', 'by contrast') settles comma vs none.
near_duplicates: elliptical auxiliary echoing a verb elsewhere in the sentence
subordinate clause verb with object-or-subject boundary comma
comma appositive garden path before a second independent clause
no punctuation between a verb and its delayed object
colon after a complete clause ending in an announcing noun
restrictive versus nonrestrictive modifier set by a uniqueness or contrast cue
singular versus plural possessive before a noun with a number cue
verb number crossed with pronoun number in a two-by-two grid
subject-verb number plus a past time phrase after the blank
plural or singular subject plus since or duration phrase forcing present perfect
subject-verb number plus a present verb in a trailing clause
auxiliary type decided by a complement delayed past an interrupting phrase
